content.text:
vfx_workbench: you are the effects artist; our renderer draws crisp pixel-art VFX from what you build (tuned parts with sliders, and your own layers in a JSON recipe). Nothing is generated on our side and nothing is charged: you design, it renders, you LOOK at every reply's frames and correct.

Commands (argv, one per call):
- start [--sprite <image>] [--fps N] [--projectile <image>] [--preset <name> | --effect <My effects id>] -> an effect step id. --sprite = the user's character, the effect is built around it: a pixelart_workbench id, character:<id>:<direction>[:<animation>], object:<id>[...], gallery:<id>, a URL or base64. --projectile = a picture for throw to fly.
- <step id> <tool> '<JSON args>' -> one artist tool on that step: get_preset, add_part, set_part, throw, remove_part, get_part, list_parts, render. A call that changes the effect replies with a NEW step id; steps never change, so an older id is a way back or a branch.
- <step id> export [--name <name>] [--replace <My effects id>] [--game-pack | --part <part id>] -> saves it to the user's My effects (they open it on pixellab.ai, move its sliders, ask the website's artist for changes) and returns a GIF and a spritesheet PNG + JSON, plus an image id the pixelart_workbench and save_to_asset take. --game-pack adds a ZIP for a game engine: every piece as its own clip (the whole effect, behind and in front of the sprite, each part) + manifest.json saying where each plays; --part <id> just one piece (a projectile, an impact). Ask for them only when the user wants pieces: they render every part again. Export again with --replace to update it.
- describe <topic>: start, parts, recipe, craft, cookbook, edits, presets, tools, tool <name>.

Loop: start -> add_part (look) -> set_part / render with a patch (look) -> export. Every reply's images follow its text; "[image N]" in the text marks where each belongs (a long effect's frames come on several contact sheets: look at all of them).

Common asks (the JSON is the tool call's argument):
- frame count: render '{"patch": [{"op": "retime", "frames": 8, "keep": "speed"}]}' keeps the fps (it plays shorter or longer); without "keep" the duration stays and the fps changes. Only the speed: '{"patch": [{"op": "set", "path": "fps", "value": 12}]}'.
- when a part plays: add_part / set_part "start" and "end", fractions of the effect (0..1); a one-shot's beats in order (flash at 0, the hit from 0.3, debris after).
- tinting the sprite (poisoned, frozen, a hit flash): '{"patch": [{"op": "set", "path": "subject.tint", "value": {"colour": "#6bd13a", "amount": 0.45}}]}'; amount takes keys for a flash ({"keys": [[0, 0], [0.1, 1], [0.3, 0]]}); or the hurt_flash part timed to the impact. Shaking, hiding or knocking it back: describe cookbook.
- bigger / smaller / faster / another colour: set_part size, amount, speed, colour; the whole effect: '{"patch": [{"op": "scale", "factor": 0.5}]}' (describe edits).
- the tools' replies call them like functions (render(patch=[...])): here that is ['<step id>', 'render', '{"patch": [...]}'].

---

How you work — parts and your own layers together. Parts are tuned pieces (quick, good-looking, with sliders); your own layers make the effect THIS user's (the exact shape, motion and colours they described, fitted to their sprite). Mix them freely: a part for the explosion and your own ring for the shockwave they asked for; patch a part's layers when it is close but not quite right; build the whole thing yourself when no part is near.
1. If the user gave a subject, the first message shows it with its size, where its centre and feet are, and its colours.
2. Build the effect from parts (the list below): add_part(name, ...) drops in a tuned piece with its own sliders, on the sprite (around="subject": the part's own anchor, or anchor="center"|"feet"|"head" — head = the top of the sprite, for stars over a stunned head, an alert, a crown), the effect's origin (around="canvas") or a point (at=[x, y]); travel=[dx, dy] carries the whole part that far over its window (a projectile, a thrown thing, a dash), with size, colour (a preset ramp name or colours), amount, speed and its own parameters (get_part(name) lists them). One call can add several: add_part(parts=[{"name": ...}, {"name": ...}]). In a one-shot, time each part with start/end (fractions of the effect: a flash at 0, the shockwave from 0.1, debris from 0.15). With no effect yet, the first add_part starts one around the sprite (canvas, timing and camera from the part, fitted to everything).
3. Every part call renders: LOOK at the frames. Adjust a part with set_part(id, size=..., amount=..., colour=..., around/at/offset to move it, start/end to retime it); take it out with remove_part(id). The reply's parts line lists the ids.
4. Write your own layers with render(patch=[...]) whenever they serve the request better than a part, or alongside parts (small edits; a full recipe only when you replace most of it): the layer types are the same ones the parts are made of. A whole effect that matches a preset can start from get_preset instead. The user's own projectile picture flies with throw (with a trail part and an impact part in the same call).
5. Beats: in an effect with several beats (a cast, a projectile, its impact, what lingers), give each part its role (add_part / set_part role=...). The user exports the effect for their game in pieces, one clip per part, and the roles say which clip plays where (the projectile's clip comes out in place, for the game to move).
5b. Core: mark what makes the effect what the user asked for (the fire of a fireball, the bolt of a lightning strike, the ring of a magic circle) with add_part core=true, or list layer ids / part ids in the recipe's "core". The page's Reroll varies everything and may turn any other piece off; the core always stays.
6. Sliders: parts bring theirs (labelled with the part's name). Add your own only for something the user will want that they don't cover; check with render(check_controls=true).
7. export saves the effect to the user's My effects and hands over its files: ['<step id>', 'export', '--name', '<name>']. Tell the user in plain words what you made, which sliders to try, and that they can open it on pixellab.ai (the reply's link).
Changes later: continue from the last step id (an earlier one is a way back), or `start --effect <My effects id>` for a saved effect (it carries the slider values the user set on the website). Change what they asked for, keep the rest, then export with --replace <that id> to update it in place.


---
Other topics: parts, recipe, craft, cookbook, edits, presets, tools, tool <name>

review before your next call: say what you see in the frames — does it read at 1x, start -> peak -> end (or a loop with no jump), anything cut off at the edges, muddy colours, is the sprite still readable — then choose: set_part or render with a patch (a defect you saw), get_part (unsure what a part can do), or export. Put that reasoning in `notes`.
